title: Magical String
statement:
The magical string `s` is an endless string over the characters `'1'` and `'2'` that describes itself: cut `s` into maximal runs of equal characters and write each run's length down in order, and the digits you get spell `s` again. It starts with `'1'`, which fixes it completely; its beginning is `"1221121221221121122..."`.

Given an integer `n`, return how many of the first `n` characters of `s` are `'1'`.
notes:
## Intuition

The string tells you how to build itself. Its runs alternate between 1s and 2s, and the k-th digit of `s` is the length of the k-th run. So once the first few digits are known, a slow pointer can read the next run length while the string grows at the end. The writer is always ahead of the reader (each run has length at least 1), so the digit being read has always been written already. A different, slower idea is to re-expand the whole known prefix again and again, since the runs a correct prefix describes form a longer correct prefix.

## Approach

1. Seed `s` with `[1, 2, 2]`. The first two runs (`1` and `22`) are already written, and `s[2] = 2` describes the third run, so set `read = 2`.
2. While `s` is shorter than `n`: the new run uses `next`, the digit that differs from the last one written, and its length is `s[read]`. Append that many copies, then move `read` forward.
3. Count the 1s among the first `n` digits in `ones` (the last run may overshoot `n` by one digit, which is ignored).

## Example 1, step by step

Start with `s = [1, 2, 2]` and `read = 2`. The last digit is 2, so `next = 1`, and `s[2] = 2` gives two of them: `s = [1, 2, 2, 1, 1]`, `read = 3`. The last digit is now 1, so `next = 2`, and `s[3] = 1` gives one: `s = [1, 2, 2, 1, 1, 2]`. The length reached 6, so the loop ends. The first six digits `1 2 2 1 1 2` contain three 1s, so the answer is `3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each loop step appends one or two digits, and counting is one pass.
- Space: O(n) for the generated digits.

## Pitfalls

- Starting the reader at index 0 or 1 rebuilds runs that the seed already contains and produces a wrong string.
- The last run can push the length to `n + 1`; count only the first `n` digits.
- For `n` up to 3 the loop never runs, so the answer must come from the seed itself.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `s` | the digits of the magical string generated so far |
| `read` | index of the digit giving the length of the next run |
| `next` | the digit used for the next run (1 and 2 alternate) |
| `k` | counts the copies appended for one run |
| `ones` | number of 1s among the first `n` digits |
| `i` | position while counting |

narration.2: Seed the string with its first three digits: the runs 1 and 22.
narration.3: s[2] is the first digit that describes a run not yet written.
narration.5: Keep growing the string until it has at least n digits.
narration.6: Runs alternate, so the new run uses the digit that differs from the last one.
narration.7: s[read] says how long the new run is.
narration.8: Write one digit of the new run at the end.
narration.10: Move the reader to the digit describing the following run.
narration.14: Look at each of the first n digits only.
narration.19: Return how many 1s the first n digits contain.
